briefs.title: New person-based measure estimates 53% of U.S. adults own their home
briefs.summary: The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis proposes the Homeowners-to-Population Ratio (HPOP), a person-based complement to the household-based owner-occupancy rate. Using American Community Survey microdata, HPOP classifies adult reference persons and their spouses or unmarried partners in owner-occupied homes as homeowners. For 2024, the researchers estimate that 53% of U.S. adults were homeowners, compared with an owner-occupancy rate of roughly 65%. HPOP sits about 12 points below the roughly 65% household-based owner-occupancy rate — the gap reflecting adults who live in owner-occupied homes without being the owner or their spouse/partner (e.g., adult children or other relatives). Among adults under 35, HPOP was about 22% — well below the roughly 37% owner-occupancy rate for households headed by someone under 35, which is a household-based measure and therefore not directly comparable. For Colorado, 2024 HPOP was 57.2% versus a 66.0% owner-occupancy rate — above the national HPOP. Because HPOP is published only at the state and metro (CBSA) levels, the available Colorado geographies are the state plus four metros: Fort Collins (HPOP 68.9%), Colorado Springs (68.5%), Denver-Aurora-Lakewood (63.2%), and Pueblo (41.5%). HPOP is not published for counties or places, so it cannot be reported for smaller Colorado jurisdictions such as Ignacio or Fruita. Source: Minneapolis Fed HPOP data, 2024.
briefs.implications: For COHO, HPOP should complement—not replace—the owner-occupancy rate. It can add person-level context to developer-oriented ownership analysis, including co-resident adults, delayed household formation, and disparities by age and demographic group. HPOP does not verify deed title for every adult, prove that co-resident adults will form separate households, or guarantee future rental demand. Local application should pair available state or metro HPOP estimates with household formation, cost burden, income, tenure, and supply data.

briefs.title: Colorado fee reductions for affordable housing: what towns waive, who pays, and how it differs by region
briefs.summary: COHO read the codes, fee schedules and council records of 46 Colorado jurisdictions and verified 115 local fee measures and 63 land-use or zoning incentives that lower the cost of affordable housing. Most fee relief is discretionary — 65 of 102 one-time fee measures need council or staff approval — and 93 of 115 fee measures do not say how the waived money is replaced. State law lets a local government waive an impact fee for low- or moderate-income or affordable employee housing (C.R.S. 29-20-104.5(5)) but does not require it, and a water or sewer utility run as an enterprise must keep grants from state and local governments under 10% of its annual revenue to stay outside TABOR. Consistent with that, utility fees are the ones cities repay from another fund: Loveland's Community Housing Development Fund repaid up to $366,070 of waived utility fees for Mirasol Phase III, while up to $504,807 of capital expansion fees on the same project were waived with no repayment, and Longmont may subsidize water and sewer system development fees only with money appropriated outside its utility funds. The regions differ. Mountain resort towns mostly waive fees outright for deed-restricted homes without an income cap — Mountain Village charges $21,650 per tap for a deed-restricted employee condo against $43,300 for a single-family home, and Telluride waives the in-town water and sewer tap attributable to a deed-restricted unit. Western Slope programs scale by income: Grand Junction waives 100% of city impact fees for rentals at or below 70% AMI, 75% at 71–80% AMI and 50% at 81–90% AMI, for a 30-year commitment. Front Range cities lean toward partial reductions, rebates after payment and income-qualified utility bill help: Colorado Springs rebates up to 100% of development charges after they are paid, Fort Collins credits up to $14,000 per unit, Littleton rebates $2,500 per affordable unit, Denver cuts the building permit fee $6,500 per income-restricted unit, and Westminster credits income-qualified households $360 a year on water bills. Deferrals (Fort Collins, Lafayette, Salida, Avon) are listed separately because a deferred fee is still owed. Screening context, not a study: what a jurisdiction offers is not what a project will receive.
briefs.implications: Four practical points. First, check who charges each fee: a town waiver may not reach a separate district — Aspen cannot waive school or sanitation district fees, and Grand Junction's program covers only city water and sewer, not Ute Water or Clifton Water. A special district has its own power to waive, amortize or defer its taps for affordable housing (C.R.S. 32-1-1001(1)(j)(II)), so the district is a separate ask. Second, count a waiver only once it is committed to the project; most are discretionary and several are subject to annual appropriation. Third, model a deferral as a loan with its trigger, not as a cost cut. Fourth, ask how a waiver is paid for: programs that name the paying fund (Grand Junction, Brighton, Loveland, Longmont) show where the money comes from; most do not. On land use, the 63 verified incentives in 37 jurisdictions are mostly inclusionary zoning with offsets, 90-day expedited review tied to the Proposition 123 fast-track, density bonuses and parking reductions. The Proposition 123 fast-track is a review deadline, not a fee rule. No Colorado statute found requires a local fee waiver for affordable housing; state bills since 2021 list fee waivers only as one optional strategy (HB21-1117, HB21-1271, HB24-1152, HB24-1313, SB24-174). Each jurisdiction's verified measures appear in its Housing Needs Assessment under local resources. The legal basis, how waived fees are paid for, the trends and numbered sources are in docs/methodology/LOCAL-JURISDICTION-HOUSING-CONTRIBUTIONS.md; the data is data/policy/fee-reductions.json.

briefs.title: HB26-1065 and Colorado’s Transit Zone credit: what the law establishes, what the draft QAP proposes, and what remains unknown
briefs.summary: Colorado HB26-1065 became law on May 27, 2026 and created Transit and Housing Investment Zones (THIZ), a state affordable-housing income-tax credit, and a separate sales-tax-increment mechanism for qualifying transit investment projects. The housing credit may be allocated by CHFA from 2027 through 2033, up to $8,333,333 annually, and is claimed over six credit years. Geographic eligibility depends on the official OEDIT THIZ map: the statute uses a two-mile zone around transportation facilities identified on that map. COHO’s tracked source was last checked September 26, 2026 and still recorded the map as not published, with publication due October 30, 2026. Transit-stop proximity therefore remains a screen, not an eligibility determination. CHFA’s 2027–2028 QAP Third Draft calls the housing credit the Transit Zone (TZ) credit. The draft says it may be awarded under a separate TZ Credit Allocation Plan in lieu of standard state credit, not in addition to it. Under the draft maximum-credit schedule, a 9% award may pair with a fixed $650,000 annual state or TZ credit in 2027 and $675,000 in 2028; a Round Two 4% award may pair with up to $675,000 annually in 2027 and $600,000 in 2028. Alternative amounts apply if the proposed state gap-funding pilot is unavailable. These are annual credit amounts, not total project proceeds, and the QAP terms are not final until adopted.
briefs.implications: The law, the OEDIT map and the QAP answer different questions. HB26-1065 creates the programs and statutory limits. OEDIT’s map determines whether an exact site is inside an eligible THIZ. CHFA’s QAP and separate allocation plan govern how an eligible rental project competes for and pairs the TZ credit. The draft QAP’s ordinary TOD/TOC location criterion is separate: it proposes five points for a qualifying site within a half-mile walk of transit, but those points do not themselves establish THIZ eligibility and are not TZ-credit-specific. The enacted bill and fiscal note do not create a distinct rural credit set-aside, bonus or enhanced rural amount; statewide geographic equity is a consideration for transit investment projects, not a substitute for zone eligibility. Until OEDIT publishes the authoritative map and CHFA adopts final rules, a project should record the exact site, retain the screen as preliminary, show TZ funding as unavailable rather than zero, and avoid adding draft credit proceeds to a development budget. The Deal Calculator reads the same canonical legislation record and displays the applicable 9% or 4% draft pairing only after supported map eligibility; it does not silently add the amount to the capital stack.

briefs.title: The permanent 12% increase in the 9% LIHTC state ceiling: what the 2025 federal law changed
briefs.summary: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1), approved on July 4, 2025, changed how much housing credit each state may award every year. Section 70422(a) of the law amends section 42(h)(3)(I) of the Internal Revenue Code. Each state has an annual housing credit ceiling: the authority its housing credit agency uses to award credits outside the tax-exempt bond route, mainly the competitive credits commonly called 9% credits. Part of that ceiling is the greater of a per-resident amount or a small-state minimum. For calendar years beginning after December 31, 2025, the amended law multiplies both of those amounts by 1.12, a 12% increase, after the annual cost-of-living adjustment. The amended provision sets no end year. The same provision previously gave a 12.5% increase for 2018 through 2021 only. For 2026, IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 sets the amount at the greater of $3.416 per resident or $3,953,600, and lists the section 70422(a) amendment among the changes it reflects.
briefs.implications: The increase applies only to the per-resident or minimum amount. The other parts of a state's ceiling, which are unused credit carried forward from the prior year, credit returned during the year, and any national-pool allocation, are not multiplied. Section 70422(a) changes the size of each state's annual credit authority; it does not change the credit rate, the income and rent tests, or the eligible-basis rules for an individual building. The law's only other change to section 42 is the tax-exempt bond-financing test in section 70422(b), which COHO tracks as a separate record. In Colorado, CHFA allocates federal housing credits and administers the program under its Qualified Allocation Plan. Colorado's total for a year depends on the state population figure used and on any carried-forward or returned credit. COHO has not verified a 2026 Colorado total published by CHFA, so this brief does not state one. The legislation record lists January 1, 2026 as the effective date of the change.

briefs.title: The 25% bond-financing test for 4% LIHTC buildings: what the 2025 federal law changed
briefs.summary: Public Law 119-21 (H.R. 1), approved on July 4, 2025, changed the tax-exempt bond test that lets a building claim housing credits without an allocation from the state's annual credit ceiling. Buildings that qualify this way receive the credits commonly called 4% credits. Section 70422(b) of the law rewrites section 42(h)(4)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code. Before the change, the test had one route: tax-exempt private activity bonds counted against the state's volume cap had to finance 50% or more of the aggregate basis of the building and the land under it. The amended provision keeps that 50% route and adds a second one. A building also qualifies if such bonds finance 25% or more of that basis, as long as one or more of those bonds come from an issue dated after December 31, 2025 and together finance at least 5% of the basis. The change applies to buildings placed in service in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. The amended provision sets no end year.
briefs.implications: A building can now meet the test with a smaller share of bond financing than before, so the same amount of volume cap can support credits for more buildings. Bonds issued before 2026 still count toward the 25%, but only when bonds from post-2025 issues together provide at least 5% of the basis; that 5% can come from more than one such bond. For a rehabilitation that is treated as a separate new building, section 70422(b)(2)(B) treats both the existing building and the rehabilitation as placed in service on the date the rehabilitation expenditures are. The change does not alter the credit rate, the income and rent tests, or the state's annual credit ceiling. The law's other change to section 42, the 12% ceiling increase in section 70422(a), has its own COHO brief. In Colorado, the Department of Local Affairs receives the state's volume cap; CHFA's December 4, 2025 stakeholder presentation says that by statute 50% goes to statewide authorities, including CHFA, and 50% to local governments. In the same presentation CHFA said new CHFA multifamily lending and 2026 Round Two projects would use not more than 45% bond financing, lower when feasible. COHO has not verified a CHFA policy for later years, so this brief does not state one.

briefs.title: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: what the 2026 federal housing law changes for affordable rental financing
briefs.summary: H.R. 6644, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, became law on July 11, 2026 as Public Law 119-101. A note by the Office of the Federal Register on the law says it was presented to the President on June 29, 2026 and became law without his signature because it was not returned within the time the Constitution allows. The House gave its final approval on June 23, 2026. The law reforms federal housing-supply and HUD programs. It does not amend section 42 of the Internal Revenue Code, so it does not change housing tax credit ceilings, credit rates or eligibility rules. Section 1202 says no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the law or its amendments.
briefs.implications: The provisions below bear most directly on financing affordable rental housing. Section 204 makes the new construction of affordable housing an eligible Community Development Block Grant activity, limited to 20% of the amounts allocated to the recipient, and only for amounts appropriated after the date of enactment. Section 501 changes the HOME Investment Partnerships program: section 501(i) repeals the rule under which a participating jurisdiction lost the right to draw HOME funds it had not committed within 24 months, and section 501(l) exempts four categories of HOME activity from review under the National Environmental Policy Act: new construction infill housing projects, acquisition of real property for affordable housing, certain rehabilitation projects, and new construction projects of 15 units or less. An infill housing project must, among other tests, sit on previously disturbed land of not more than 5 acres. HUD must issue any rules it determines necessary for the exemptions within 1 year of enactment. Section 405(a) lets a voucher unit in a housing tax credit building meet the Housing Choice Voucher inspection requirement if it was physically inspected and met the suitability-for-occupancy requirement in section 42(i)(3)(B)(ii) during the preceding 12 months, and the public housing agency performed that inspection itself or can obtain its results. COHO searched the Federal Register on October 11, 2026 and found no HUD rule or notice putting the section 204 or section 501 changes into effect, so this brief does not describe how HUD will apply them. COHO has not verified any Colorado grantee's plan to use the new CDBG activity.

briefs.title: Colorado's local-government right of first refusal and right of first offer (HB24-1175): what it requires through 2029
briefs.summary: Colorado House Bill 24-1175, approved by the Governor on May 30, 2024 and effective August 7, 2024, gives local governments two rights to buy certain multifamily rental properties. It adds sections 29-4-1201 to 29-4-1208 to the Colorado Revised Statutes. Under section 29-4-1202, the city, town or county where the property is located has a right of first refusal, exercised with a matched offer, on a rental property of 5 units or more that is existing affordable housing, meaning it is subject to a recorded restricted-use covenant or similar affordability agreement. Under section 29-4-1203, it has a right of first offer on other rental properties of at least 15 units and not more than 100 units, which the seller must notify it about before engaging a licensed broker to find buyers or listing the property on the multiple listing service. Either right may be used only to keep or convert the property as long-term affordable housing, which the act defines to include affordability for at least 40 years; the right of first offer also allows a mixed-income development. Under section 29-4-1207 both rights terminate on December 31, 2029, except that a process the local government began before that date continues until it concludes. Section 29-4-1208 repeals the part on July 1, 2031.
briefs.implications: For a covenant-restricted property, including one financed with housing tax credits, the seller must notify CHFA and the local government at least 2 years, and again at least 6 months, before the last affordability restriction expires. When a sale is in prospect, the seller must notify the local government within 14 calendar days of a triggering event, such as signing a letter of intent, listing the property, or conditionally accepting an offer. The local government is to tell the seller within 14 calendar days of receiving that notice whether it intends to preserve or waive its right of first refusal, and then has 30 calendar days to make an offer, and must agree to close within 60 calendar days after the seller accepts, or within the period in a third-party buyer's all-cash offer if the seller has one. If the price in the seller's notice drops by 5% or more, or its terms or conditions materially change, the seller must give notice within 7 days and the local government may exercise or re-exercise the right. The local government and the seller may extend any of these periods by written agreement. The right of first offer does not apply if the property's first certificate of occupancy was issued within the 30 years before the listing. Section 29-4-1205 exempts several kinds of transfer, including a sale by a seller that has applied for, is in the process of, or has completed a resyndication or recapitalization under a public affordable housing program, if the seller gives the local government notice and evidence of it; the rights apply again if that effort fails. A local government may assign either right to a local or regional housing authority or to CHFA. Under section 29-4-1206 the remedies are damages and statutory penalties against the seller: a court must award at least $10,000 for a first material violation and at least $30,000 for a later one, and no more than $100,000, and a buyer taking title through the seller takes it free of these rights. COHO has not verified which Colorado local governments have waived or assigned their rights, so this brief does not list them.
